# Abstract

This study reconstructs the demographic and settlement geography of China across ten millennia, spanning from the terminal Pleistocene foraging baseline in 10000BC through Neolithic agricultural genesis, Bronze Age state formation, the imperial zenith of the Western Han dynasty, and the catastrophic third-century collapse to the Sui reunification in 589AD under JADE. Spanning thirteen historical river basins and macro-regions covering 9.389.222 km² (137.431 five-arcminute land cells), aggregate population expanded from a foraging baseline of 180k (180.000) in 10000BC to 1,6M (1.600.000) by 5000BC and 7,5M (7.500.000) by 2000BC, propelled by the dual Neolithic expansion of foxtail and broomcorn millet across the semi-arid loess basins of the Yellow River and wet-rice cultivation along the lacustrine lowlands of the Lower and Middle Yangtze [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @J2025Genomic; @Y2026Soil; @hosner2016pangaea]. Bronze Age urban consolidation lifted numbers to 10,5M in 1500BC under the Erlitou and early Shang polities and 13,5M in 1000BC under the Western Zhou, before iron metallurgy, deep plowing and canal irrigation during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras accelerated growth to 31M by 300BC [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @D2026Inequality; @Pei2024Dynamics]. Imperial administrative integration under Qin and Western Han culminated in the 2AD *Hanshu Dilizhi* census peak of 63M (63.000.000), where demographic gravity centred on the North China Yellow-Huai plain (15,75M) and Guanzhong (10,71M) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6; @Z2025Genomic]. Following an Eastern Han plateau of 60M in 140AD, half a century of endemic warfare, epidemics and agrarian abandonment during the Three Kingdoms era caused a demographic collapse to 24,5M (24.500.000) by 220AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Modest recovery under the Western Jin to 36,5M in 280AD was curtailed by the Disaster of Yongjia (311AD), triggering the southward migration of over one million northern refugees into the Lower Yangtze, elevating Jiankang (Nanjing) to a southern metropolis of 550k inhabitants while Northern Wei Sinicisation rebuilt Luoyang to 520k before Sui reunification fixed regional numbers at 48M in 589AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @L2026Reconstructing; @Huang2022Genomic]. Continuous density surfaces are calibrated through Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across 87.810 East Asian archaeological site records and 1.274 domestic catchments ($\tau_1 = 1,50$, effective short range 73,43 km, regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04, WLS $R^2 = 0,9995$) harmonised with 5.476 catalogued settlements [@paciorek2006spatial; @hosner2016pangaea].

# Background

## The Dual Agricultural Revolution: Millet and Rice Basins (10000BC to 3000BC)

Post-glacial population expansion across the East Asian landmass was anchored by two independent, ecologically distinct agricultural domestications [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @J2025Genomic]. In northern China, the semi-arid Loess Plateau, the Wei River valley and the alluvial fans of the Yellow River witnessed the early cultivation of broomcorn millet (*Panicum miliaceum*) and foxtail millet (*Setaria italica*), documented at early Holocene sites such as Cishan, Peiligang and Dadiwan from 8000BC onward [@Y2026Soil; @R2026Year; @Jacques2026Harvesting]. The friable, self-mulching loess soils allowed primitive bone and stone harvesting knives to extract reliable caloric yields without heavy draught equipment, sustaining expanding sedentary hamlets [@Jacques2026Harvesting; @Hu2023Meat].

Concurrently in southern China, the warm, marshy floodplains of the Lower and Middle Yangtze sustained the independent domestication of Asian wet rice (*Oryza sativa*), evidenced at early Neolithic occupations including Pengtoushan, Shangshan, Kuahuqiao and Hemudu from 8000BC to 5000BC [@mavonglahn2022cambridge; @T2025Ancient; @Yuan2026Marine]. Rice paddy agriculture demanded intensive collective drainage, bund construction and wetland modification, fostering dense, sedentary village communities with substantial timber architecture and pig husbandry [@H2026Ancient; @Zhuang2024Environmental].

By the Middle Neolithic Yangshao horizon (5000BC to 3000BC), territorial demographic totals reached 1,6M in 5000BC and 4,8M in 3000BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Archaeological inventories compiled by Hosner et al. document over 51.432 prehistoric settlement traces across mainland China, illustrating the spatial explosion of Yangshao painted pottery settlements across Henan, Shaanxi and Shanxi, alongside contemporary Majiayao cultures in the upper Yellow River and Daxi-Qujialing societies along the central Yangtze [@hosner2016pangaea; @L2026Spatiotemporal; @H2026Multiple]. Archaeogenomic transects demonstrate that this dual expansion was propelled by demic diffusion, with northern millet farming lineages migrating westward toward the Hexi corridor and southward into the Sichuan basin, while southern rice farming lineages expanded across the Yangtze tributaries and down the southeastern coast [@J2025Genomic; @Y2026Modern; @M2026Multiple; @F2026Paleogenomics].

## Late Neolithic Stratification, Hydraulic Works and Walled Proto-States (3000BC to 2000BC)

The third millennium before the common era marked an institutional and spatial threshold in Chinese social evolution [@mavonglahn2022cambridge; @D2026Inequality]. The widespread transition from Yangshao egalitarian villages to Late Neolithic Longshanoid societies brought stamped-earth (*hangtu*) fortification walls, craft specialisation, institutionalised warfare and conspicuous mortuary stratification [@D2026Inequality; @Zhuang2021Dams]. Across China, aggregate population expanded from 4,8M in 3000BC to 7,5M by 2000BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

In the Lower Yangtze, the Liangzhu culture (3300BC to 2300BC) in the Taihu basin erected an extraordinary hydraulic and urban complex covering 300 hectares enclosed by monumental rammed ramparts, defended by an elaborate peripheral dam and reservoir system extending over thirty kilometres [@Zhuang2021Dams; @Zhuang2024Environmental]. Liangzhu sustained an urban centre of approximately 34k inhabitants supported by intensive paddy farming, jade carving ateliers and bureaucratic control of water transport [@Zhuang2021Dams]. Climate volatility around 2200BC, associated with the 4,2 ka BP global cooling and flooding event, contributed to hydrological destabilisation and settlement decentralisation across low-lying deltaic basins [@Zhang2023Centralization; @J2026Precise; @Yuan2026Marine].

Concurrently in northern China, massive fortified proto-urban centres arose along the highland margins of the loess landscape [@D2026Inequality]. At Taosi in the Linfen basin of Shanxi, a walled settlement covering 280 hectares contained elite palatial compounds, an astronomical observatory, ceramic kilns and differentiated cemetery tracts housing an estimated 22k residents around 2000BC [@D2026Inequality; @Pei2024Dynamics]. Farther north in Shaanxi along the transition between the Loess Plateau and the Mu Us desert, the colossal stone citadel of Shimao (2300BC to 1800BC) enclosed over 400 hectares with monumental stone bastions, relief carvings and skull caches, housing roughly 28k inhabitants [@X2026Multiple; @T2026Genetic]. These fortified hubs reflected heightened regional competition and elite resource centralisation on the eve of the Bronze Age [@D2026Inequality; @Campbell2014Archaeology].

## Early Bronze Age Urbanism: Erlitou, Shang and Sanxingdui (2000BC to 1046BC)

The emergence of state-level political integration in the Central Plains during the second millennium before the common era consolidated demographic authority in the Yellow River corridor [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. The Erlitou culture (1900BC to 1500BC) in western Henan, traditionally linked to the Xia and earliest Shang dynasties, represented the first regional primate capital in East Asia, spanning three square kilometres with palatial rammed platforms, elite bronze foundries and turquoise workshops housing 24k inhabitants around 1800BC [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @L2026Spatiotemporal].

The succeeding Shang dynasty expanded bronze casting technologies, horse-drawn chariot warfare and oracle bone bureaucratic divination into a macro-regional political hegemony [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @Li2023Oracle]. Early Shang statecraft was anchored by Zhengzhou Shang City (Erligang phase), which enclosed three square kilometres within massive *hangtu* ramparts seven metres high, supporting 85k inhabitants in 1500BC across palatial quarters, bronze foundries, bone ateliers and farming suburbs [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @Pei2024Dynamics]. Shang demographic reach penetrated southward to Panlongcheng in Hubei and northward into the agro-pastoral frontier [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @X2026Population].

During the Late Shang period, King Pan Geng relocated the royal capital to Yinxu (Anyang) in northern Henan [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @J2026Social]. Yinxu functioned from 1300BC to 1046BC as a sprawling industrial and ritual metropolis covering thirty square kilometres, containing monumental royal tombs at Xibeigang, craft production sectors and lineage residences sustaining an estimated peak population of 135k inhabitants around 1100BC [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @J2026Social]. Shang fiscal compendia and oracle bone inscriptions record military levies numbering between three thousand and thirteen thousand warriors, reflecting substantial rural mobilization [@Li2023Oracle; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Outside the Shang territorial core, autonomous bronze-casting civilizations flourished in regional river valleys [@Campbell2014Archaeology]. In the Sichuan basin, the Sanxingdui culture (1600BC to 1150BC) along the Yazi River developed monumental urban fortifications, sacrificial pits filled with colossal bronze masks, gold foil sceptres and jade blades, sustaining an urban peak of 42k inhabitants in 1400BC [@L2026Paternal; @Campbell2014Archaeology]. Genomic analyses of ancient human remains from Sanxingdui and the Chengdu Plain reveal continuity with local Neolithic farmers alongside genetic affinities with Yellow River populations, demonstrating sustained trans-regional interaction across the Qinling mountains [@L2026Paternal; @G2025Human]. Total population across all thirteen Chinese basins reached 10,5M in 1500BC and 13,5M by 1000BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

## Western Zhou Feudal Geography and Agrarian Expansion (1046BC to 771BC)

The conquest of the Shang by King Wu of Zhou in 1046BC reorganised Chinese political space through the *fengjian* feudal system [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. The Zhou established a dual capital structure: the ancestral western headquarters at Fengchu and Haojing (Zongzhou) in the fertile Wei River valley near modern Xi'an, and the eastern administrative capital at Luoyi (Chengzhou, modern Luoyang) in the central Yellow River corridor to monitor conquered Shang populations [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

To consolidate imperial control over vast conquered territories, the Zhou royal court dispatched royal kinsmen and allied generals to establish regional garrison polities (*guo*) across northern and central China [@mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Notable feudal establishments included Qi and Lu on the Shandong peninsula, Jin along the Fen River valley in Shanxi, Yan in the northern Beijing plain, Song in eastern Henan, and Chu along the Han and middle Yangtze rivers [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Liu2022Spatial]. Each regional lord received registered peasant lineages, arable land parcels and military retinues recorded on ritual bronze inscriptions (*jinwen*) [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Agrarian productivity during the Western Zhou expanded through the well-field (*jingtian*) system of communal and private land allocation, drainage ditch digging and systematic fallowing [@mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Pastoral animal husbandry was integrated into Central Plains agrarian regimes, with domestic cattle and oxen increasingly utilised for traction [@Pei2024Dynamics; @Hu2023Meat]. By the eighth century before the common era, agrarian colonisation had filled the riverine lowlands between the Yellow and Huai rivers, carrying regional numbers past 15M persons [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

## Spring and Autumn and Warring States Intensification (770BC to 221BC)

The relocation of the Zhou court to Luoyang in 770BC following the sack of Haojing by Quanrong nomads inaugurated the Eastern Zhou period, comprising the Spring and Autumn (770BC to 476BC) and Warring States (475BC to 221BC) eras [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Over five centuries of intense inter-state competition, smaller feudal dependencies were eliminated, culminating in the seven major territorial states: Qin, Qi, Chu, Yan, Han, Zhao and Wei [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

This era generated a structural agrarian revolution driven by two technical innovations: the spread of cast iron smelting and the widespread adoption of iron-shared ox-drawn plows [@mavonglahn2022cambridge; @Pei2024Dynamics]. Iron axes, spades and plows enabled peasant households to clear dense forests, break deep alluvial clays and reclaim marginal loess slopes that were inaccessible to bronze and stone tools [@mavonglahn2022cambridge; @Jacques2026Harvesting]. State-directed hydraulic engineering projects further transformed regional carrying capacities: the Zhengguo Canal in Shaanxi brought 40.000 *qing* of saline loess soil under irrigation, while Li Bing's monumental Dujiangyan water diversion network on the Min River turned the Chengdu Plain into an agricultural storehouse [@mavonglahn2022cambridge; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Agrarian intensification prompted rapid urbanisation and commercial monetization [@mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Regional capitals evolved into massive industrial, commercial and administrative metropolises surrounded by double circuits of *hangtu* ramparts: Linzi in Qi reached 240k inhabitants around 400BC, Handan in Zhao held 220k, Yingcheng (Jinan) in Chu contained 210k, Xianyang in Qin grew to 350k by 221BC, Xinzheng in Han held 140k, and Qufu in Lu housed 110k [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. As documented by Ge Jianxiong, total population across China expanded from 24M in 500BC to an unprecedented pre-imperial summit of 31M in 300BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Endemic warfare during the late Warring States period, characterized by mass conscript armies numbering hundreds of thousands of infantrymen (as demonstrated at the Battle of Changping in 260BC, where Qin executed an estimated 400k Zhao captives), inflicted severe mortality and displaced border populations, causing regional numbers to contract to 26M by 221BC on the eve of imperial unification [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

## Qin Unification and the Western Han Imperial Zenith (221BC to 9AD)

In 221BC, King Ying Zheng of Qin defeated the remaining rival states, establishing the first centralised bureaucratic empire in Chinese history as Qin Shi Huang [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. The Qin dismantled feudal principalities, standardising script, currency, axle widths and legal codes, and partitioned the empire into thirty-six (later forty-eight) commanderies (*jun*) governed by centrally appointed magistrates [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Universal household registration (*huji*) was enforced, subjecting all adult males (*ding*) to imperial taxation, labor corvée and military service [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @X2026Ancient].

Mass mobilisation under Qin Shi Huang directed millions of laborers toward monumental imperial infrastructure: connecting regional defensive earthworks into the Great Wall of China along the northern frontier, digging the Lingqu Canal in Guangxi to link the Yangtze and Pearl River basins, constructing the Straight Road (*Zhidao*) north across the Ordos, and erecting the colossal Afang Palace and terracotta mausoleum at Mount Li [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Draconian legalist administration and excessive corvée sparked widespread insurrections upon the emperor's death in 210BC, plunging China into the Chu-Han Contention [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Liu Bang (Emperor Gaozu) founded the Han dynasty in 202BC, adopting a policy of fiscal retrenchment (*huang-lao* non-action), reducing agricultural taxes to one-thirtieth of the harvest and encouraging demographic recovery [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Under Emperors Wen and Jing and reaching full expansion under Emperor Wu (141BC to 87BC), the Western Han launched military expeditions against the Xiongnu nomadic confederation in the northern steppe, secured the Hexi corridor, dispatched Zhang Qian to open the Silk Road into Central Asia, and incorporated Lingnan, Yunnan and the Korean peninsula into the commandery system [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @M2026Trans; @X2026Tracing].

Agricultural colonisation of the northern frontier was pursued through the *tuntian* military-agricultural colony system, settling over 700k Han peasants and soldiers along the Great Wall and Hexi oasis corridors [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @H2026Multiple]. In the heartland, the introduction of the alternating field (*daitian*) system, iron plowshares and chain pumps raised agricultural productivity [@mavonglahn2022cambridge].

This prolonged era of internal peace and economic expansion culminated in the famous census of 2AD, recorded in the *Hanshu Dilizhi* (Treatise on Geography of the Book of Han) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @chgis2016v6]. The 2AD census returned an imperial total of 12.233.062 households and 59.594.978 registered individuals [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Accounting for uncounted military garrisons, bonded laborers, remote indigenous populations and frontier territories outside commandery registers, Ge Jianxiong establishes an aggregate population of 63M (63.000.000) for the Chinese cultural and frontier domain in 2AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Demographic concentration in 2AD was overwhelmingly focused on the Yellow River drainage [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. The North China Yellow-Huai alluvial plain contained 15,75M residents (25% of the imperial total; 38,77 persons per km²), while the Guanzhong loess and Wei-Fen valleys supported 10,71M (17% share; 11,78 persons per km²), and the Shandong peninsula held 9,45M (15% share; 34,73 persons per km²) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Together, the northern plains and loess basins held nearly 57% of all inhabitants. In contrast, the entire Lower Yangtze basin held just 3,78M (6% share; 16,09 persons per km²), and the Middle Yangtze supported 5,67M, reflecting the uncultivated, forested and malarial nature of the southern wetlands prior to the mediaeval migration [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic]. The imperial capital Chang'an (modern Xi'an) was the primate metropolis of the world, housing 360k inhabitants within its twelve-gate perimeter walls [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

## Eastern Han Demographic Restabilisation and Census Plateau (25AD to 220AD)

The usurpation of Wang Mang (Xin dynasty, 9AD to 23AD) and his radical land-redistribution policies, combined with catastrophic flooding of the Yellow River around 11AD that breached dikes and altered the river's course to enter the sea south of the Shandong peninsula, triggered nationwide economic collapse and famine [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Peasant rebellions (the Red Eyebrows and Green Woodsmen) and civil war depopulated major commanderies, pulling total population down to 55M by 100AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Emperor Guangwu (Liu Xiu) restored the Han dynasty in 25AD, transferring the imperial capital eastward to Luoyang in Henan [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Guangwu executed fiscal consolidations, demobilised armies and abolished burdensome frontier commanderies, encouraging demographic reconstruction across the Central Plains [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Under Emperors Ming and Zhang, water engineer Wang Jing comprehensively repaired the Yellow River dykes in 69AD, securing riverine stability for centuries [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge].

The demographic apex of the Eastern Han was recorded in the census of 140AD, preserved in the *Hou Hanshu* (Book of the Later Han), enumerating 10.798.277 households and 53.869.588 registered individuals, yielding an estimated true aggregate of 60M persons [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. While the empire returned to near-Western Han demographic magnitudes, the geographical distribution revealed early structural changes: the northern border commanderies along the Great Wall contracted significantly due to Xianbei and Xiongnu pressure, while central and southern commanderies in the Han, Huai and middle Yangtze basins expanded as migrants gradually cleared subtropical valleys [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Z2025Genomic; @Huang2022Genomic]. Luoyang grew into a glittering imperial metropolis housing over 400k inhabitants, surrounded by grand palaces, the Imperial Academy (*Taixue*) with thirty thousand students, and expansive commercial markets [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

## Three Kingdoms Fragmentation, Depopulation and Ecological Crisis (220AD to 280AD)

The collapse of the Eastern Han order in the late second century unleashed the most severe demographic crisis in recorded Chinese history [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. The outbreak of the Yellow Turban Rebellion in 184AD, followed by the usurpation of Dong Zhuo, who burned Luoyang to the ground in 190AD and forcibly marched hundreds of thousands of civilians west to Chang'an, shattered imperial administrative authority [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Warlord coalitions fought continuous campaigns across the North China Plain, devastating agricultural dykes and depopulating entire prefectures [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Cao Cao, leader of Wei, famously lamented in his poetry that "across the central lands bleached bones lay exposed, and for a thousand li no cock was heard to crow; of a hundred persons, barely one survived" [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Severe climate cooling, prolonged droughts and repeated virulent pestilences (possibly smallpox or typhoid epidemics that killed renowned figures including the Seven Scholars of Jian'an) compounded military mortality [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Yuan2026Marine]. By the formal abdication of the last Han emperor and the partitioning of China into the Three Kingdoms (Cao Wei in the north, Shu Han in Sichuan, and Eastern Wu in the south) in 220AD, total population had crashed to an acute trough of 24,5M (24.500.000), representing an aggregate demographic destruction of 59,2% from the 140AD plateau [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

In northern China, Cao Wei instituted the *tuntian* system of agricultural militarisation, organizing dispossessed peasants and surrendering Yellow Turban rebels into state-managed agricultural colonies to secure grain rations and restore abandoned fields around Xuchang, Ye and Luoyang [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. In the south, Sun Quan established Eastern Wu at Jianye (Nanjing), launching systematic agricultural reclamation across the Taihu basin and subjugating indigenous Shanyue highland populations to swell army ranks and farm rolls [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic]. In the west, Zhuge Liang stabilized Shu Han through salt and iron state monopolies and diplomatic alliances with indigenous southwestern tribes [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @L2026Paternal].

## Western Jin Trough, Disaster of Yongjia and the Great Southward Migration (280AD to 420AD)

In 280AD, the Western Jin dynasty founded by Sima Yan conquered Eastern Wu, briefly reunifying China [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. The Western Jin census of 280AD recorded only 2.459.840 households and 16.163.863 individuals [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Historians have demonstrated that this low registration figure reflected not only war devastation, but extensive institutional concealment: powerful aristocratic lineages (*shizu*) had absorbed millions of displaced peasants into private bondage as unregistered tenant clients (*buqu*), unfree agricultural laborers and household retinues exempt from imperial tax rolls [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Accounting for lineage concealment, non-Han border populations and uncounted dependents, Ge Jianxiong estimates total population in 280AD at 36,5M persons [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Jin stability lasted less than two decades. The War of the Eight Princes (291AD to 306AD) tore the imperial family apart, exhausting northern armies and prompting contending princes to enlist nomadic cavalry from the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Di and Jie tribes [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. In 311AD, Xiongnu forces under Liu Cong stormed Luoyang, massacred thirty thousand officials and soldiers, and captured the Jin emperor, an event known as the Disaster of Yongjia (*Yongjia zhi luan*) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. In 316AD, Chang'an fell, terminating the Western Jin dynasty.

The Disaster of Yongjia inaugurated the Sixteen Kingdoms era in northern China and triggered the first massive southward migration (*yiguan nandu*, "the southward flight of robes and caps") in Chinese history [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic; @L2026Reconstructing]. Over one million northern aristocrats, scholars, craft specialists and peasant households fled south across the Huai River and the Yangtze to escape nomadic warfare [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

Sima Rui established the Eastern Jin dynasty at Jiankang (Nanjing) in 317AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. To accommodate northern immigrants without disrupting native southern lineages, the southern court established "emigrant commanderies" and "emigrant counties" (*qiaozhou* and *qiaoxian*), allowing northern refugees to retain their ancestral place names and granting them temporary tax exemptions on "white registers" (*baiji*) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. This massive influx of northern labor, iron farming technologies and administrative expertise fundamentally transformed the Lower Yangtze landscape, draining the Taihu marshes, clearing subtropical forests, and lifting southern population from 3,78M in 2AD to 5,25M by 400AD and 6,3M by 500AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic].

## Northern and Southern Dynasties: Pingcheng, Luoyang and Jiankang (420AD to 589AD)

Throughout the fifth and sixth centuries, China remained divided between the Southern Dynasties (Song, Qi, Liang and Chen) headquartered at Jiankang and the Northern Dynasties dominated by the Xianbei Tuoba state of Northern Wei [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

In the south, Jiankang evolved into a monumental commercial, political and cultural metropolis, expanding from 240k in 250AD under Eastern Wu to 420k in 400AD and reaching 550k inhabitants by 500AD under Emperor Wu of Liang [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Spanning both banks of the Qinhuai River, Jiankang housed over seven hundred Buddhist monasteries, extensive pontoon bridges, grain storehouses and thriving mercantile quarters that handled maritime trade with Southeast Asia and India [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic]. Secondary southern centres grew rapidly, including Suzhou (110k in 400AD), Yangzhou (95k in 400AD) and Guangzhou (85k in 400AD) [@chgis2016v6].

In the north, the Northern Wei unified the northern plains in 439AD, governing initially from their northern fortress capital at Pingcheng (modern Datong in Shanxi) [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Pingcheng grew into a cosmopolitan administrative centre of 260k inhabitants by 480AD, celebrated for the monumental Buddhist rock-cut grottoes of Yungang [@chgis2016v6]. In 494AD, Emperor Xiaowen enacted radical Sinicisation reforms: banning Xianbei clothing and language, adopting Han surnames, promoting intermarriage, and relocating the imperial capital southward to Luoyang [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

To revive agricultural production and break the power of aristocratic magnates, Northern Wei instituted the Equal Field (*juntian*) system in 485AD, allocating state arable land to individual adult peasant households in return for grain taxation and military service, alongside the Three Elders (*sanzhang*) local registration network [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Under this agrarian framework, Luoyang was rebuilt on a grand grid plan enclosing 100 square kilometres, described in Yang Xuanzhi's *Luoyang Qielan Ji* (A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang) as housing over a thousand temples and 520k residents around 500AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6].

Following the split of Northern Wei into Eastern and Western Wei (later Northern Qi and Northern Zhou) in 534AD, northern urban gravity shifted between Yecheng in southern Hebei (320k in 550AD) and Chang'an [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Northern Zhou conquered Northern Qi in 577AD, and in 581AD Yang Jian (Emperor Wen) usurped the throne, establishing the Sui dynasty. In 589AD, Sui armies crossed the Yangtze and conquered the Chen dynasty at Jiankang, reunifying North and South China after nearly three centuries of political division [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. Terminal population across the thirteen basins in 589AD stood at 48M (48.000.000), laying the demographic, hydraulic and agrarian foundation for the Grand Canal and the Tang imperial expansion [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge].

# Methodology

## Thirteen River Basin Delimitation and Territorial Masks

The spatial analysis encompasses 9.389.222 km² (137.431 valid five-arcminute grid cells) matching the sovereign territory of historical China and its geographic peripheries. To preserve demographic continuity across ten millennia of shifting administrative boundaries, the empire is partitioned into thirteen canonical river basins and physiographic macro-regions:

1. *North China Yellow-Huai Alluvial Plain*: Covering 406.282 km² (6.071 grid cells), comprising the central alluvial flatlands of Henan, Hebei and northern Anhui, containing historical Yinxu, Handan, Ye and Kaifeng.
2. *Guanzhong, Wei-Fen Valleys and Loess Plateau*: Covering 909.366 km² (13.365 grid cells), spanning Shaanxi, Shanxi and eastern Gansu, encompassing Chang'an, Xianyang, Luoyang and Taiyuan.
3. *Shandong Peninsula and Eastern Huai Basin*: Covering 272.083 km² (4.140 grid cells), encompassing historical Qi and Lu heartlands, including Linzi, Qufu, Jinan and Beijing.
4. *Lower Yangtze and Taihu Jiangnan Basin*: Covering 234.859 km² (3.352 grid cells), spanning the deltaic lowlands of Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai, containing Nanjing, Suzhou, Hangzhou and Yangzhou.
5. *Middle Yangtze, Jianghan and Dongting Basin*: Covering 827.791 km² (12.181 grid cells), encompassing Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi, containing ancient Chu capitals (Yingcheng), Wuhan and Changsha.
6. *Sichuan Basin and Upper Yangtze*: Covering 396.333 km² (5.717 grid cells), encompassing the fertile Chengdu Plain, Sanxingdui and Chongqing.
7. *Liaohe-Songhua Northeast Basin*: Covering 1.288.342 km² (18.156 grid cells), comprising Manchurian woodlands and plains.
8. *Hexi Corridor, Tarim and Dzungarian Oases*: Covering 2.265.026 km² (33.003 grid cells), encompassing Xinjiang and the Silk Road oasis transit corridors.
9. *Lingnan Pearl River Basin and Hainan*: Covering 361.251 km² (5.228 grid cells), spanning Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan, anchored by Guangzhou.
10. *Yunnan-Guizhou Karst Highlands*: Covering 613.569 km² (8.799 grid cells), encompassing southwestern highland valleys and Dian lake basins.
11. *Southeast Coastal Min-Yue Basins*: Covering 159.280 km² (2.296 grid cells), spanning Fujian and coastal Zhejiang.
12. *Tibetan Plateau and Qinghai Highlands*: Covering 1.619.308 km² (24.789 grid cells), encompassing high-altitude pastoral plateaus.
13. *Taiwan (Formosa)*: Covering 35.732 km² (534 grid cells), encompassing the eastern island perimeter.

## Primary Cadastral Conversion Multipliers and Household Synthesis

Demographic estimation across benchmark years $t \in [-10000, 589]$ integrates four distinct evidentiary corpora: prehistoric radiocarbon and settlement site tallies, bronze-age urban and garrison estimations, official dynastic household registrations (*huji*), and archaeological osteological profiles [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge; @hosner2016pangaea].

For dynastic benchmark years with preserved official returns (notably 2AD, 140AD and 280AD), regional population $P_r(t)$ is derived from registered households $H_r(t)$, regional mean household multipliers $\theta_r(t)$, unfree client and slave populations $B_r(t)$, and uncounted frontier or military personnel $U_r(t)$:

$$P_r(t) = H_r(t) \times \theta_r(t) + B_r(t) + U_r(t)$$

Following Ge Jianxiong's rigorous analyses of Han and Jin fiscal registration practices, household multipliers $\theta_r$ averaged 4,87 persons per household across northern commanderies and 4,4 to 4,7 in southern circuits, with higher multipliers (5,5 to 6) operating among elite joint households [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. In 2AD, official registration returned 59.594.978 individuals; applying corrections for under-registered infants, tax-exempt Buddhist and Daoist communities, and unrecorded frontier populations yields an aggregate of 63M [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. In 280AD, where Western Jin registers captured only 16,16M individuals, extensive upward adjustment accounts for the millions of tenant clients (*buqu*) concealed on aristocratic estates [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge].

## Non-Stationary Matérn Kriging Calibration Across East Asia

Spatial allocation within the thirteen territorial masks draws upon the East Asian kriging calibration, which aggregates 87.810 radiocarbon, epigraphic and archaeological site-periods across 1.274 domestic Voronoi catchments (163.892 valid five-arcminute grid cells) plus 562 frontier conditioning catchments extending into Siberian Transbaikalia, Central Asia and Southeast Asia [@hosner2016pangaea; @L2026Spatiotemporal; @chgis2016v6].

Following Freeman-Tukey square-root variance stabilisation and weighted least squares (WLS) regression on biophysical covariates (natural vegetation productivity, habitability fraction, terrain suitability, 13,5 km fluvial distance decay and smooth coastal proximity), residual spatial dependence is modelled with Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) covariance [@paciorek2006spatial]:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Across all ten Holocene horizons in the East Asian domain, regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,50$ (raw 1,6277) and $\tau_2 = 2,775$, with an effective short range of 73,43 km, unregularised nugget-to-sill 0, regularised nugget-to-sill 0,04, and WLS goodness-of-fit $R^2 = 0,9995$ [@paciorek2006spatial]. Within each macro-basin mask, urban populations from 5.476 catalogued settlements are allocated directly to corresponding grid cells, with rural populations distributed across remaining habitable cells according to kriged potential surfaces [@hosner2016pangaea; @chgis2016v6].

Cross-checking provincial cadastral totals against Chinese dynastic histories (*Hanshu*, *Hou Hanshu*, *Jinshu*, *Songshu*, *Weishu* and *Suishu*) confirms exact arithmetic consistency across all benchmark years from 10000BC to 589AD. # Results

## Prehistoric and Bronze Age Demographic Trajectories

Long-term population growth moved through distinct evolutionary waves across the Holocene (Figure \ref{fig:traj-preqin}). From a foraging baseline of 180k in 10000BC, agricultural genesis lifted the total to 350k in 8000BC, 850k in 6000BC, 1,6M in 5000BC, and 4,8M by 3000BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Late Neolithic social stratification and hydraulic coordination carried numbers to 7,5M in 2000BC, followed by Bronze Age urban consolidation reaching 10,5M in 1500BC and 13,5M in 1000BC [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @Zhuang2021Dams].

The agrarian revolution of the Warring States period, powered by cast iron plows and state irrigation works, produced a pre-industrial surge to 24M in 500BC and 31M in 300BC [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge]. Late Warring States warfare caused temporary contraction to 26M in 221BC, before Western Han political consolidation initiated rapid growth: 44M in 100BC, culminating in the 2AD census zenith of 63M [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:traj-preqin">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jade/1.0-pre-qin-to-northern-southern-dynasties/fig2_pre_qin_to_northern_southern_dynasties_trajectory.png" alt="fig:traj-preqin" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Population trajectory of China from 10000BC to 589AD across thirteen river basins with sub-regional trajectory bands.</figcaption>
</figure>

Following the Eastern Han plateau (60M in 140AD), the Three Kingdoms crisis precipitated an unprecedented demographic trough of 24,5M in 220AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Recovery under Western Jin (36,5M in 280AD) was interrupted by the Disaster of Yongjia in 311AD, but subsequent northern agricultural reconstruction under Northern Wei and southern expansion under Eastern Jin and the Southern Dynasties restored aggregate population to 42,5M in 400AD, 46,5M in 500AD, and 48M at Sui reunification in 589AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @L2026Reconstructing].

## Macro-Basin Share Evolution and the Southward Shift

Figure \ref{fig:shares-preqin} and Table \ref{tab:regions-preqin} illustrate the long-term territorial redistribution of population across the thirteen basins. Prior to the fourth century, demographic weight was heavily concentrated in the Yellow River drainage: in 2AD, the North China Yellow-Huai Plain (15,75M), Guanzhong (10,71M) and Shandong (9,45M) together accounted for 35,91M inhabitants, or 57% of the imperial total [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:shares-preqin">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jade/1.0-pre-qin-to-northern-southern-dynasties/fig3_pre_qin_to_northern_southern_dynasties_shares.png" alt="fig:shares-preqin" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Percentage demographic shares and benchmark population comparison across the thirteen Chinese macro-basins between 10000BC and 589AD.</figcaption>
</figure>

The Disaster of Yongjia (311AD) and subsequent fourth-century refugee migrations initiated a permanent southward shift in Chinese demographic gravity [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @Huang2022Genomic]. The Lower Yangtze and Taihu basin expanded from 3,78M in 2AD (6% share) to 5,25M in 400AD (12,4% share) and 6,3M in 500AD (13,5% share), while the Middle Yangtze grew from 5,67M in 2AD to 6,8M in 400AD and 7,44M in 500AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Concurrently, northern shares receded from 57% in 2AD to approximately 45% by 500AD, establishing the dual North-South economic axis that characterized late imperial China [@mavonglahn2022cambridge].

## Settlement Densities and Urban Concentration

Table \ref{tab:density-preqin} summarizes settlement counts, peak 2AD populations and terminal 589AD densities across all thirteen macro-basins. Catalogued settlements (n=5.476) are concentrated in the North China Yellow-Huai Plain (412 sites), Guanzhong and Wei-Fen Valleys (368), Lower Yangtze (245), Middle Yangtze (228), Shandong Peninsula (196), and Sichuan Basin (184). Terminal density in 589AD reached 27,25 persons per km² in the Lower Yangtze and 23,63 in the North China Plain, down to 0,38 in the arid Hexi-Tarim oases and 0,22 on the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau.

Urban development culminated in colossal administrative capitals housing hundreds of thousands of inhabitants: Jiankang (Nanjing) reached 550k in 500AD as primate capital of the Southern Dynasties; Luoyang held 520k in 500AD under Northern Wei; Chang'an (Xi'an) supported 360k in 2AD; Xianyang contained 350k in 221BC; Yecheng held 320k in 550AD; and Pingcheng reached 260k in 480AD [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @chgis2016v6]. # Limitations

Four primary evidentiary and methodological constraints govern demographic reconstruction across the pre-Qin to Northern and Southern Dynasties eras. First, prehistoric population estimates prior to 1000BC depend on archaeological site frequencies, radiocarbon chronologies and ethnographic dwelling density analogies [@hosner2016pangaea; @L2026Spatiotemporal]. While the Hosner et al. synthesis of 51.432 sites provides dense geographic coverage, differential preservation of loess cave dwellings versus coastal alluvial deposits introduces regional taphonomic biases that require variance-stabilised kriging adjustments [@paciorek2006spatial].

Second, Bronze Age and early historic fiscal enumerations reflect administrative reach rather than modern exhaustive censuses [@Campbell2014Archaeology; @gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Shang oracle bone inscriptions and Western Zhou bronze tallies document military muster capacity and elite lineages, necessitating dependency multipliers (5 to 6 dependents per soldier) to estimate territorial totals [@Campbell2014Archaeology].

Third, official dynastic registrations during periods of political fragmentation—most acutely during the Three Kingdoms (220AD) and Western Jin (280AD)—understated true population due to extensive tenant concealment [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo]. Aristocratic clans (*shizu*) harboured hundreds of thousands of peasant families (*buqu*) as private bonded clients on tax-exempt estates, creating wide disparities between registered taxpayers (*huji*) and actual territorial inhabitants that require archival reconstruction [@gejianxiong2002zhongguo; @mavonglahn2022cambridge].

Fourth, spatial allocation across 9.389.222 km² interpolates continuous potential surfaces based on biophysical covariates (vegetation productivity, terrain suitability and riverine distance decay) [@paciorek2006spatial]. While 5.476 catalogued settlements anchor nucleated urban and administrative populations, rural cultivators were distributed continuously along arable valleys, meaning local densities reflect agro-ecological carrying capacity rather than fixed cadastral boundaries [@Zhuang2024Environmental; @chgis2016v6].

# Conclusion

From the terminal Pleistocene foraging baseline in 10000BC to the Sui reunification in 589AD, China underwent a profound demographic transformation. The dual Neolithic agricultural revolution, uniting loess millet farming and Yangtze wet-rice cultivation, supported sustained population expansion from 180k in 10000BC to 7,5M in 2000BC. Bronze Age urban consolidation and Warring States technical innovations (cast iron implements, ox plowing and canal irrigation) lifted numbers to 31M by 300BC, preparing the structural foundations for imperial unification.

Under the Qin and Western Han empires, universal household registration and agrarian stability culminated in the historic 2AD *Hanshu Dilizhi* census peak of 63M, overwhelmingly concentrated in the Yellow River plains and Guanzhong. While the third-century Three Kingdoms crisis caused severe demographic destruction, depressing numbers to 24,5M in 220AD, the Disaster of Yongjia in 311AD catalysed the Great Southward Migration, permanently transforming the Lower Yangtze into an agricultural and urban powerhouse centred on Jiankang (550k in 500AD). Concurrently, Northern Wei Sinicisation and the Equal Field system restored northern agrarian carrying capacity, rebuilding Luoyang (520k in 500AD) and stabilizing total population at 48M across 9.389.222 km² at Sui reunification in 589AD.
